newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Ashdown, UK leader doomed to play third fiddle.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Ashdown, UK leader doomed to play third fiddle.

text.p: In his pink shirt and bright tie, Paddy Ashdown looks incongruous standing in a tin shed at a livestock market, surrounded by red-faced farmers.
He has flown in from London and in an hour he will climb aboard his bus for the next stop on the election campaign trail for his Liberal Democrat party.

At 56, Ashdown is the oldest of the leaders of the main parties in Britain's May 1 general election, and he has been on the road for a month. But he is determined to keep going, even though no one -- except Ashdown -- seriously believes he can win power.
Ashdown is convinced any slip, any loss of concentration, could signal to the ever-present media pack that he is not up to the job of prime minister.

His party musters only about 15 percent in opinion polls, and the chances of a Liberal Democrat victory are worse than slim. Ashdown's best hope seems to be in a hung parliament where his party could hold the balance of power.

This scenario has never deterred Ashdown in his eight years as leader of the Liberal Democrats. He remains convinced British politics are about to shift away from its two-party dominated system, opening the way for his party.
"What on earth do you think I'm doing here, playing ping-pong?" he once rounded on an interviewer who suggested he could never become prime minister.
LIBERAL DEMOCRATS FLOURISHING UNDER ASHDOWN

The Liberal Democrats have flourished since Ashdown became leader in 1988. At that time the party, reeling from a brief but damaging alliance with the even smaller Social Democrat Party, was plagued by infighting and running a hefty deficit.
Now it has more seats on local councils than any party except Labour -- the main opposition party at Westminster -- and in the 1992 election it won nearly 18 percent of the vote.

Under Britain's first-past-the-post electoral system, it won only 20 seats in the 651-seat parliament. Not surprisingly, the Liberal Democrats are wedded to the idea that Britain must embrace proportional representation.

Ashdown, who served with the royal marines in Borneo and Belfast before becoming a diplomat and then a politician, scored a major coup when he seized the constituency of Yeovil from the ruling Conservatives in 1983. It had taken him seven years of trying.
The craggy-faced former commando begins each day with an early morning news conference before criss-crossing Britain for speeches and photocalls and meet-the-people opportunities.

When Labour leader Tony Blair and Conservative Prime Minister John Major were considering holding television debates, the Liberal Democrats threatened to sue if Ashdown was not allowed to take part. In opinion polls, however, he rates a consistent third when voters are asked who would make the best prime minister.
Today Ashdown is in the west of England, the Liberal Democrats' strongest territory.

His features crease in concentration as he discusses treatments for blowfly and sheep scab with sceptical-looking farmers, and he has to raise his voice to be heard over animal cries and a loudspeaker announcing the sale of autumn lambs.

The farmers shuffle uncomfortably on the hard seats that have been placed around a carpeted stage, backed with slick grey screens bearing the party's logo, to create a mini-television studio in the smelly barn.

Soon Ashdown finds himself on difficult ground, as farmers air their hostility to the European Union (EU), which they blame for crippling Britain's beef industry by banning exports because of mad cow disease (BSE). The Liberal Democrats are fervently pro-European.
The party leader is keen to divert the farmers' ire to the Conservative government's handling of the BSE crisis.
"I will get back to you later," he tells one farmer who wants to complain about the power of the EU. "Now has anybody got anything else to say about BSE?"
LIBERAL DEMOCRATS PLEDGE TO RAISE TAXES
Ashdown's tendency to take the moral high ground infuriates Major and Blair, who say that he doesn't have to deal with the reality of politics as they do.
"You end as pious and pompous as you have been throughout this Parliament," Major spluttered at Ashdown in an angry outburst in parliament after the election was called.
Blair said his party would no longer have been in the running if it had matched Ashdown's grandiose pledges.
The Liberal Democrats are the only major party to have pledged to raise income tax, saying they will spend the money on improving state education.
They have also promised to raise more money for the health service by increasing the tax on every packet of cigarettes by five pence (eight cents).

After 18 years in opposition, Labour has been fighting hard to shed its old "tax-and-spend" image and has pledged not to increase the top and bottom rates of income tax for five years if it is elected, so the Liberal Democrat pledges present a stark contrast.
But if he is loathed by his rivals, Ashdown appears to be popular with the voters -- more popular than his party, according to opinion polls.
Ashdown's greatest moment came during the 1991 Gulf War, when television companies were keen to make use of his military experience and he became a valued interpreter of events.
The following year, in the months before the 1992 general election, revelations of an affair with a former secretary threatened his upright image.

But Ashdown at once admitted and apologised for the affair, his wife, Jane, stood by him and the other woman turned out to be respectably middle-aged. Ashdown's star rose rather than fell because of his honesty over the affair but he has never shaken off the tabloid title "Paddy Pantsdown". ($ = 0.615 British Pounds)
